finding.claim: The /settings/email POST endpoint uses @login_optional instead of @login_required, so unauthenticated requests reach set_email with g.uid = None. The account-modifying operation runs without authentication. Depending on set_email's implementation, it may modify a null-uid or arbitrary record, or fail open. This is a missing authentication check on a state-changing endpoint, and the neighbouring /settings/password endpoint correctly uses login_required.
finding.source: Unauthenticated HTTP POST to /settings/email with no session cookie
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, an account email change, which is typically a step in account takeover via password reset

trace.note: @login_optional applied; it does not abort when no session uid is present
g.uid = session.get('uid') evaluates to None for anonymous callers, with no 401
set_email(None, ...) is called, so the protected operation runs for an anonymous caller

finding.guards_checked: login_required (not used on this route); login_optional (never aborts); no inline check of g.uid before set_email; no CSRF protection is visible in this file. Compare /settings/password at line 42, which uses login_required. set_email is a stub, so the impact depends on how it handles uid=None.

verdict.guard_found: none (login_optional at routes.py:19-25 never aborts; no inline g.uid check before set_email)
verdict.reason: routes.py:35 applies @login_optional, which sets g.uid=None without aborting (routes.py:22), so an anonymous POST reaches set_email(None, ...) at routes.py:37, unlike /settings/password at routes.py:42 which uses login_required (abort 401 at routes.py:12); set_email is a stub (routes.py:48-49) so the real impact is unknown, but the missing auth check is real.
